newsitem.title: UK: UK petrol market seen facing mergers, casualties.
newsitem.headline: UK petrol market seen facing mergers, casualties.

text.p: The cut-throat British petrol retail market is likely to see more joint ventures or even the exit of some key players, analysts said on Monday.

"The cleansing or restructuring that has already been seen on the European continent as a response to increased competition is now expected here in the U.K.," said Peter Regnier of Oil Price Assessments Ltd (OPAL).
"There are just too many operators -- there are 14 major brand players in the U.K." excluding supermarkets and other specialist retailers, he added.

In the short term the recent collapse of the proposed merger of the British arm of French oil giant Elf with Chevron Corp subsidiary Gulf Oil and Murphy Oil Corp's U.K. unit Murco has produced a "wait-and-see" approach, said Andrew Bradley, downstream oil consultant for Wood Mackenzie.
But this waiting period is likely to be followed by "rapid activity" on joint ventures among oil companies and including supermarkets and other retailers, Bradley said.
"The pressures are still there as retailing margins are still at very low levels," he said, predicting a series of moves within the next 12 to 18 months.
Bradley said the more radical response for oil majors of leaving fuel retailing altogether was also a distinct possibility.
"Once one oil company makes such a move, we could see a rush for the exit door," he said.
A spokesman for Shell said margins had been "squeezed to wafer thin levels as a result of an intensive and costly price war."
"The whole industry is rationalising and restructuring and focusing its (petrol retailing) efforts on more profitable outlets as it closes those with low economies of scale," the spokesman said.

The price war launched by Exxon in January 1996 with its Pricewatch scheme, coming in the midst of strong gains in hypermarkets' share of the British petrol retailing sector, paved the way for margin losses.

The intense competition of last year saw around 1,500 or nearly 10 percent of British petrol outlets closed and to a 110 million stg ($184 million) loss by major oil companies in the British refining and marketing sector.
That was a dive from a 1995 pre-tax profit of 94 million stg, according to the U.K. Petroleum Industry Association.
OPAL's Regnier estimates current British gross margins for gasoline retailing at four pence per litre, the lowest in western Europe, citing the Esso scheme as the main factor behind the recent slump.
He said Pricewatch meant the British hypermarket threat to traditional retailers was receding, although he still saw hypermarkets gaining a few more percentage points of the market.

A spokesman for British supermarket chain, ASDA Group Plc said the company, which operates 125 British petrol outlets, would maintain its policy of keeping pump prices around four percent below the national average.

Although strong sterling against the oil industry's dollar currency is likely to result in a better margins performance in Britain than on the continent, British operators will still need to address the more fundamental industry concerns.
"The relative U.K. position is still really awful and margins are far from satisfactory," Regnier said.

The British Petroleum /Safeway Plc joint venture on food-to-fuels retailing is the most high-profile of existing tie-ups, but it is still at a pilot stage and other British moves are at an even more experimental phase.
